cards.prompt:
AI helpers answer fast and sound sure. But every answer is a **prediction**: the model's best guess from the patterns it learned. Sounding sure isn't the same as being right, so check important things with a source you trust.

You're using an AI helper to write a short piece about your town's old bridge.

steps.text: The AI says the bridge opened in **1952**. It sounds very sure. What do you do?

choices.text: Write it down: it sounds certain
choices.consequence: A reader writes in: the bridge opened years later. Confident isn't the same as correct.

choices.text: Check a trusted source, like a local history book
choices.consequence: Good thinking. Let's see what it says.

choices.text: Ask the AI if it's sure
choices.consequence: It says "Yes, I'm sure!" An AI can say it's sure and still be wrong, because it can't be sure its own answer is right.

steps.text: The local history book says the bridge opened in **1958**. What now?

choices.consequence: Right: you checked a source you trust and caught the AI's mistake.

choices.text: Use 1952: the AI has read far more than one book
choices.consequence: Reading a lot doesn't make each answer checked. The AI made a guess; the book's date was checked by people.

cards.hint: The AI's answer is a guess. How could you find out whether it's right?
cards.explanation: An AI's answer is a **prediction**, so even a confident one can be wrong. Asking the AI again doesn't help: it can't be sure its own answer is right. Check important facts with a **trusted source**, and go with the source.

cards.prompt:
A chatbot tells you, calm and certain, that a film came out in 2009. It actually came out in 2011.

Why can an AI sound so sure and still be wrong?

options.text: It predicts from patterns, and can't check if it's true
It's trying to fool you on purpose, to seem clever
options.nudge: AI doesn't have plans or feelings. Think about how it makes an answer.

options.text: It only sounds sure when it's right, so it misread you
options.nudge: Sounding sure doesn't come from being right. What is every answer an AI gives?

options.text: It looked the date up in its list of facts, which was old
options.nudge: A model doesn't keep a list of facts to look up: it learned patterns from examples. So what is each answer?

cards.hint: What is every answer an AI gives you: a fact, or something else?
cards.explanation: Every answer is a **prediction** from the patterns it learned. It doesn't check whether the answer is true, so it can sound just as sure when it's wrong as when it's right. It isn't lying, and it isn't reading from a list of facts.

cards.title: A program, not a person
cards.body:
A chatbot can sound caring, but it can't notice if you're not OK.

If something's worrying you, talk to a **trusted adult**, a friend, or, in Australia, **Kids Helpline (1800 55 1800)**, free, any time. If you're in danger right now, call **000**. A chatbot can be somewhere to start your thoughts, never instead of real people.

cards.prompt: Your photo app sorts pictures by who's in them.

steps.text: It labels a picture of your friend as someone else, and suggests sharing it with that person. What do you do?

choices.text: Share it: the app knows best
choices.consequence: Now someone else has your friend's photo. Apps can mislabel faces, so check before you share.

choices.text: Fix the label, and don't share it
choices.consequence: Good: you caught the app's mistake before it spread. Matching a face is a prediction, so it can be wrong.

choices.text: Keep the label: the app has seen your friend's face lots of times
choices.consequence: Seeing a face many times doesn't make every match right. Matching a face is a prediction, and this one is wrong.

cards.hint: The app's label is a prediction. What do you do with a prediction before acting on it?
cards.explanation: Face matching is a **prediction**, so it can mislabel people. Check before acting on it: fix the label and don't share. The app is still useful; just don't trust its guesses blindly.

cards.prompt:
AI is handy for quick, low-stakes jobs, where a mistake is easy to spot and fix. Big decisions about people need a **person** to decide and be responsible.

Is each job **fine for AI to help with**, or does it **need a person** to decide?
cards.hint: Ask: if the AI got it wrong, would someone be hurt or treated unfairly?
cards.nudge: Look again at the jobs where a mistake would really affect someone's life.
cards.explanation: Spelling, photos and songs are low-stakes: a mistake is easy to spot and fix. Punishments, medical treatment and jobs are **big decisions about people**, so a person must decide and be responsible, even if AI helps.

cards.prompt: Match each AI limit to an example of it.

pairs.right: Calls a yellow apple a banana
Tags your friend as someone else
An AI decides a student's punishment

cards.hint: Each example comes from this module. Which limit explains what went wrong in each one?
cards.nudge: Think about each example's story: was the problem missing examples, false confidence, a mislabelled face, or a big decision?
cards.explanation: The yellow apple shows a model **only knows its examples**; the wrong year shows it can **sound sure when wrong**; the photo app shows it can **mislabel people**; and an AI deciding a punishment is a problem because it **can't be responsible**: a person must decide.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- AI gives **predictions**, not facts. Check important things.
- Big decisions about people need a person.
- Worried? Talk to a trusted adult or Kids Helpline (1800 55 1800).

Next: the module quiz.
